# Turkish NLP Datasets and Tools {#sec-turkish-resources}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Appendix status: drafted.** A catalogue of Turkish corpora, models and
tooling — the practical companion to @sec-turkish-nlp, which explains *why*
morphologically rich languages are hard rather than *what* to download. Every
link here was checked in September 2026.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**This page rots faster than any other in the book.** Model names change,
repositories are archived, and licences are revised. Treat it as a map of what
*kinds* of resource exist and check each before committing to it.
:::

## Corpora {#sec-turkish-resources-corpora}

Licence is a column of its own because it is usually the reason a dataset
cannot be used — in class or in a product.

| dataset | task | size | licence | link |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| XL-Sum Turkish | summarization | 27,176 train / 3,397 test | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | [`csebuetnlp/xlsum`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/csebuetnlp/xlsum) |
| Turkish product reviews | sentiment | ~235k reviews | CC BY 4.0 | [`fthbrmnby/turkish_product_reviews`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/fthbrmnby/turkish_product_reviews) |
| WikiANN (Turkish) | NER | 20k train / 10k test | ODC-BY | [`unimelb-nlp/wikiann`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/unimelb-nlp/wikiann) |
| SQuAD-TR | question answering | translated SQuAD | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | [`boun-tabi/squad_tr`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/boun-tabi/squad_tr) |
| UD Turkish BOUN | dependency parsing | ~9.7k sentences | CC BY-SA 4.0 | [UD\_Turkish-BOUN](https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_Turkish-BOUN) |
| WMT newstest tr-en | machine translation | 3,000 pairs per year | research use | via `sacrebleu` (@sec-machine-translation) |

: Turkish corpora used or referenced in this book {tbl-colwidths="[22,16,20,16,26]"}

Three cautions, each of which this book demonstrated on one of these datasets
rather than in the abstract.

**Check for contamination before quoting a score.** @sec-sequence-labeling
found **13.06%** of WikiANN Turkish's test set sitting verbatim in its own
training split — in a resource used by hundreds of papers. Hashing test inputs
against training inputs takes four lines.

**Check whether the benchmark was written in Turkish or translated into it.**
SQuAD-TR is translated, and that is fine as long as you say so: it measures
competence on translationese, which has different word order, sentence length
and vocabulary from text a Turkish speaker wrote.

**Read the non-commercial clauses.** `NC` in a licence means the dataset cannot
be used in a commercial product, which is discovered surprisingly late in
surprisingly many projects.

## Tokenizers and morphological analyzers {#sec-turkish-resources-tools}

@sec-turkish-nlp-analysis argues that a stemmer carries most of the retrieval
benefit and an analyser is a requirement you should be able to justify. This is
the shortlist for both.

| tool | what it does | state |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [`snowballstemmer`](https://snowballstem.org/) | rule-based Turkish stemmer, ~100 lines | maintained; took recall@1 from 28.0% to 95.3% in @sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval |
| [`zemberek-nlp`](https://github.com/ahmetaa/zemberek-nlp) | the reference Turkish toolkit — morphology, spelling, tokenization | Java, and no longer actively developed; still the most complete thing available |
| [`zeyrek`](https://github.com/obulat/zeyrek) | pure-Python morphological analyzer, a partial Zemberek port | lightly maintained; the easiest way to get real analyses in Python |
| [`turkish-morphology`](https://github.com/google-research/turkish-morphology) | Google's finite-state analyzer | archived; useful as a second opinion, not as a dependency |
| [`trnlp`](https://github.com/brolin59/trnlp) | analysis plus **generation** of inflected forms | maintained; reach for it when you need to *produce* forms, not just parse them |

: Turkish morphology tooling {tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

[Several well-known Turkish analyzers are unmaintained, and it is better to
know that now than mid-project.]{.hl} Zemberek in particular is still the best
coverage available and is not receiving fixes; plan for that rather than
discovering it when a bug matters.

For tokenization specifically, the finding that decides most projects is in
@sec-text-as-data and @sec-turkish-nlp: a multilingual tokenizer spends
noticeably more tokens on Turkish, and that ratio is fixed at pretraining time.
Measure fertility on your own text before choosing a model, because it is a
procurement decision rather than something you tune later.

## Pretrained models {#sec-turkish-resources-models}

| model | kind | note |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [BERTurk](https://huggingface.co/dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased) | encoder, 110M | the default Turkish encoder; @sec-sequence-labeling and @sec-classification fine-tune it. Use the **cased** variant — see @sec-turkish-nlp-normalization for what uncasing does to `İ` |
| [mBERT](https://huggingface.co/bert-base-multilingual-cased) | encoder, 177M | the multilingual comparison in @sec-turkish-nlp-decide, where it won on a Wikipedia-derived task despite tokenizing Turkish 19% worse |
| [TURNA](https://huggingface.co/boun-tabi-LMG/TURNA) | encoder-decoder, 1.1B | Turkish-specific generative model from Boğaziçi, built on UL2. **Released for non-commercial academic research only** — the clearest example on this page of a model you can benchmark and cannot ship |
| [Kanarya](https://huggingface.co/asafaya/kanarya-2b) | decoder, 2B | Turkish generative model; small enough to run locally |
| [`ytu-ce-cosmos`](https://huggingface.co/ytu-ce-cosmos) | several | Yıldız Technical University's Turkish model family, including GPT-2 and Llama derivatives |
| [`Trendyol`](https://huggingface.co/Trendyol) | several | industry-released Turkish LLMs; check licence terms, which vary more than international releases |

: Turkish and multilingual checkpoints {tbl-colwidths="[24,16,60]"}

The question to ask about each, and the reason this table gives no rankings:
**what was it trained on, and can you use it?** Licence terms on regionally
released models vary far more than on the big international ones, and a model
you cannot deploy commercially is not a candidate — however good its
benchmark numbers.

This table deliberately does not carry a licence column, and that is a limit
rather than a decision: for the families listed — `ytu-ce-cosmos`, `Trendyol` —
the licence varies *per model*, and derivatives of Llama carry Llama's terms
rather than their publisher's. A column would have to be wrong for at least one
row. Read the model card before you build on it, and note the date you read it.
TURNA above is the case that catches people: a good model, freely downloadable,
and not licensed for the product you were planning.

## Benchmarks {#sec-turkish-resources-benchmarks}

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [Mukayese](https://github.com/alisafaya/mukayese) | Turkish baselines across tasks, assembled [@safaya2022mukayese] because the field kept reporting Turkish numbers that could not be compared with each other |
| [TDD — Türkçe Doğal Dil İşleme](https://tdd.ai/) | Turkish corpora, models and tools collected in one place; the best single starting point |
| [`turkish-bert`](https://github.com/stefan-it/turkish-bert) | the BERTurk models with their corpora and training documented — read it for what "trained on Turkish" actually meant |

: Catalogues and baselines {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

Those three are a catalogue, a baseline collection and a model repository —
useful, and none of them is a current benchmark for a Turkish LLM. The suites
that are arrived after 2024, and they answer Mukayese's original complaint
directly:

| benchmark | what it measures | native or translated |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **TurkishMMLU** (2024) | multi-task knowledge, ~10k high-school questions across nine subjects | native — written from Turkey's national curriculum rather than translated |
| **TR-MMLU** (2024) | multi-task knowledge, 6,200 questions across 62 categories including law and health | native, sourced from standardised exams |
| **Cetvel** (EACL 2026, [`KUIS-AI/cetvel`](https://github.com/KUIS-AI/cetvel)) | 23 tasks in seven categories, **generative as well as multiple-choice** — grammatical error correction, machine translation, questions rooted in Turkish history and idiom | native and adapted |
| **TurkBench** (2026) | general Turkish LLM evaluation | native |

: Turkish LLM benchmarks, 2024 onwards {tbl-colwidths="[22,54,24]"}

Cetvel is the one to start from if you are comparing models, and the reason is
the distinction this book keeps returning to: TurkishMMLU and TR-MMLU are
multiple-choice, so they rank models on *knowledge*, and a Turkish system in
production usually fails on *generation*. A benchmark that only asks questions
with four options cannot see the failure you are going to have.

Before quoting any score from any of these, run @sec-turkish-nlp's control:
feed the scoring script a perfect prediction and confirm it returns a perfect
score. @sec-summarization found the standard ROUGE implementation mutilating
**44.4%** of Turkish words, and it was caught exactly that way and by nothing
else.

## Contributing {#sec-turkish-resources-contributing}

This page is reviewed once a semester, before the course begins, and that is
not often enough — a link here may already be stale.

If you find a dead link, a changed licence, an archived repository or a
resource that should be listed, open a GitHub issue with `[resources]` in the
title. Include what you found and when you checked it; a dated observation is
worth more than a correction with no date, which is the same argument
@sec-governance makes about regulatory instruments.
